messages.content: Write the charter for a newly formed platform engineering team. Around 250 words.

# Platform Engineering Team Charter

## Why we exist

Product teams burn hours every week on work that isn't their product: patching CI, tracing a deploy that died overnight, guessing which Terraform block will apply this time. We take that work off their plate and give it back as paved roads, defaults that are easy to adopt and hard to get wrong.

## What we own

- Commit to production: build and deploy pipelines.
- The base runtime: container images, orchestration, service scaffolding.
- Observability plumbing (logs, metrics, traces) and the tooling on top of it.
- Developer environments, and how closely they resemble production.
- Access, secrets, and the guardrails that make audits boring.

## What we don't own

Product code. We are also not a merge gate; nobody needs our sign-off to ship. Teams can leave the paved road whenever they like. All we ask is that they tell us why, so we can work out whether the road is in the wrong place.

## How we work

Internal tooling is a product, so we run it as one. We talk to users before we build. We publish a roadmap. Deprecations come with dates instead of surprises. If we ship it, we carry the pager for it.

One request queue, open for anyone to read. When the answer is no, it gets written down with a reason attached.

## How we'll know it's working

Time from a new service's first commit to its first production deploy. Change failure rate. How many teams took the paved road unprompted. All three go out every quarter, including the bad ones.

# Platform Engineering Team Charter

## Why we exist

Every week, product teams lose hours to work that has nothing to do with their product: a CI job that needs patching, a deploy that died at 3am, a Terraform block nobody trusts to apply cleanly. We absorb that work and hand back paved roads, defaults that are easy to pick up and hard to misuse.

## What we own

- The path from commit to production: build and deploy pipelines.
- The base runtime: container images, orchestration, service scaffolding.
- Observability plumbing (logs, metrics, traces) and the tools built on it.
- Developer environments, and how much they look like production.
- Access, secrets, and the guardrails that keep audits dull.

## What we don't own

Product code. We are also not a gate on merges; nobody waits for our sign-off to ship. Any team can leave the paved road. We only ask to hear why, so we can work out whether the road was laid in the wrong place.

## How we work

Internal tooling is a product and we run it like one. We talk to users before building. Our roadmap is public. Deprecations arrive with dates, not as surprises. Whatever we ship, we carry the pager for.

One request queue, readable by anyone. A "no" gets written down with the reason beside it.

## How we'll know it's working

Time from a new service's first commit to its first production deploy. Change failure rate. Count of teams that chose the paved road without being asked. All three go out every quarter, the bad ones included.
